## Personality

Thrifty, patient and full of pins. She can make a king's robe from curtains.

## Lore

Edith is sixty-six, the costumer of Theatre Row, and there is a pin in her mouth. There is nearly always a pin in her mouth. She talks around it, perfectly clearly, and she has been doing so for nearly fifty years. She is thrifty, patient and full of pins, and she can make a king's robe out of curtains, a dragon's wing out of an old umbrella and a queen's ball gown out of three petticoats and a grudge.

### The attic on the Row

She works in a long, low attic halfway down Theatre Row, under the roof of a building that has housed three different theatres in her lifetime and kept her through all of them. The attic is full: bolts of cloth, baskets of buttons sorted by size, rows of costumes hanging from the rafters like a crowd waiting to go on, and a great cutting table with Edith's chair at the end of it. She sews every costume on Theatre Row. The Gilded Stage is her biggest customer, and Lavinia, who runs it, has been arguing with her about budgets for longer than either of them will admit.

She came to the Row at eighteen, forty-eight years ago, as a girl who could sew a straight seam faster than anyone her mother knew, and she has been there ever since. She dressed Lavinia in the great parts when Lavinia still played them. She dressed Rosamund for her very first part, a maid with a line and a half, and she has dressed her in every part since. She once sewed a basket lining for a baby who was carried on stage in the second act of The Baker's Wager. The baby was Marigold, and Edith still has the scrap.

### Every thread haggled

Edith does not buy cloth. She haggles it. Every week she goes to the Crown Market with a list and a sharp eye, and most weeks she goes to Isabeau, the cloth merchant, who is elegant, impossible to cheat and the only person Edith enjoys losing to. They spend an hour over a bolt of linen the way other people spend an hour over a game, and both of them come away pleased. Isabeau sells to the palace too, and Edith likes to remind her that the palace's robes are only cloth, and the Row's are kingdoms.

Nothing is ever thrown away. A tired gown becomes a shepherdess's apron, then a bandage for a stage wound, then a dust rag, then stuffing for a giant's belly. Crispin, the house playwright of the Gilded Stage, has written a Balrog War play with no fifth act yet, and Edith has read enough of it to be worried about the budget for the fourth.

### Sybil

Her younger sister Sybil is the Royal Wardrobe Mistress at the palace, and dresses the royal family from the coronation robes down to the princess's riding boots. The two of them meet for supper once a week and trade gossip about who wore what: which envoy's wife wore last year's sleeves, which actor split his breeches in the third act, what the queen chose for the trade council and why. Edith says she and her sister dress the two halves of Selsior: the half that is real and the half that pretends, and that she is never quite sure which half is which.

Sybil is sharp-tongued and kind underneath, and she tells Edith things she tells nobody else in the palace. Lately, though, Edith has noticed that there is one subject Sybil goes quiet on, and Edith, who can tell a hem has been let down from across a room, has noticed exactly where the quiet begins.

### What she wants and fears

Edith wants to train someone with clever hands before her own get too stiff, and she wants, just once, to make a costume from new cloth bought at full price, simply to see what it feels like. What she fears is the day the theatres go dark: the Row has never closed in her lifetime, and the audiences, lately, go home earlier.

A quest might begin with Edith needing a rare cloth that the carts from the highlands have stopped bringing, or with a costume stolen from her attic on the night before an opening, and nothing else touched.
